title: On World Polio Day, Nadda Warns Polio-Free India Must Stay Vigilant
excerpt: India's last wild polio case was in January 2011 and WHO certified the country polio-free in 2014. With the virus still endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan, health leaders say the drops cannot stop.
body:
• Marking World Polio Day on October 24, Union Health Minister J. P. Nadda said India must remain vigilant against poliovirus importation despite its polio-free status.
  • India recorded its last wild poliovirus case on January 13, 2011, in Howrah, West Bengal, and the WHO certified the country polio-free on March 27, 2014.
  • Wild poliovirus remains endemic in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan, and the WHO warns a polio-free country can be re-infected through importation where immunisation gaps exist.
  • For parents: polio has no cure and protection comes from completing the full vaccine schedule — check the immunisation card and take under-fives to campaign rounds; do not skip doses because India is polio-free.

Twelve years after the World Health Organization certified India polio-free, Union Health Minister J. P. Nadda used World Polio Day on Saturday, October 24, to make a deliberately uncelebratory point: the status survives only if vaccination does.

"India's polio-free status, certified by WHO in 2014, is a testament to our sustained commitment to immunisation."

— J. P. Nadda, Union Health Minister, on X

Nadda added that India must remain vigilant against the risk of poliovirus importation and strengthen efforts to protect every child. Chief ministers made the same argument in state after state on Saturday — Madhya Pradesh's Mohan Yadav, Odisha's Mohan Charan Majhi, Rajasthan's Bhajan Lal Sharma and Delhi's Rekha Gupta all urged parents to ensure no eligible child misses the drops.

How the milestone was won

India's last wild poliovirus case was reported in Howrah, West Bengal, on January 13, 2011. The Pulse Polio Immunisation Programme, launched in 1995, put oral vaccine drops into every child under five on national immunisation days, door to door, year after year; inactivated polio vaccine joined the schedule in 2015. On March 27, 2014, the WHO certified the entire South-East Asia Region, India included, polio-free — an outcome once widely doubted for a country of India's density and geography.

https://x.com/JPNadda/status/2113847031278244180

Why the risk is importation, not history

Globally, wild poliovirus cases have fallen by more than 99% since 1988, from an estimated 350,000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to two endemic countries today: Pakistan and Afghanistan. That geography is precisely India's problem. The WHO's polio fact sheet states the mechanism plainly: as long as a single child remains infected, children in all countries are at risk, because the virus can be imported into a polio-free country and spread rapidly among unimmunised people. India runs continuous vaccination teams along its borders with Pakistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and Myanmar for exactly that reason. The disease itself allows no second chances: polio mainly affects children under five, there is no cure, and one in 200 infections leads to irreversible paralysis — an absolute figure worth holding against any sense that a certified country can relax.

What parents should actually do

Doctors marking the day, including in coverage medically reviewed by internal medicine specialist Dr Tushar Tayal, gave the same practical answer to the question polio-free status invites — can we skip the drops? No. Protection comes from completing the schedule, not from a single dose. Check a child's immunisation card against the schedule advised by the paediatrician or nearest health centre, take children under five for drops during campaign rounds, and seek medical attention promptly for any sudden weakness or paralysis in a child, which is how surveillance catches an imported case early. World Polio Day is observed every October 24, the birthday of Jonas Salk, who developed the first polio vaccine. The eradication it celebrates is real; Saturday's message from India's health leadership is that it is also rented, and the rent is due at every immunisation round.
